proposals.relationship: Morton argues that Creighton’s Laurentian narrative cannot unite Canada when it leaves Quebecers, easterners, westerners and working people outside its national ideal.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1979 address distinguishes the validity of Creighton’s account of Confederation from its limitations as a unifying myth. Own 2000 p. 19 returns to the restricted elite geography. This is Morton’s judgment, not a finding that Creighton’s original books were freshly read.
primary_locators: 1979 CHA reformatted PDF p. 5: paragraphs beginning Rejection of national moulds and Yet even to recall, through a nullity; 2000 printed pp. 18–19, especially paragraph beginning The dramatic growth.

proposals.relationship: Morton questions whether the limited-identities framework named by Careless can supply an adequate account of Canada as a whole without a new synthesis.
proposals.evidence_note: The 1979 criticism targets fragmentation within a framework explicitly attributed to Careless; it is not a claim that Careless personally advocated every grievance Morton describes. Morton welcomes the framework’s insights, methods and wider participation, and his 2000 p. 19 praises its fit with diverse experience. Careless’s 1969 original remains unread.
primary_locators: 1979 reformatted PDF pp. 6–7: By their overdue integration through the following three paragraphs on benefits, price and narrowness; conclusion pp. 9–10 on a new synthesis; 2000 printed p. 19.

proposals.relationship: Morton credits Ramsay Cook, alongside David Kwavnick, for analysis of the Task Force on National Unity report used in his 1979 address.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit own acknowledgment in note 4. Preserve Kwavnick’s shared credit; no claim that Cook supplied the entire address, endorsed its conclusions or was Morton’s teacher.
primary_locators: 1979 reformatted PDF p. 11, note 4, keyed to the earlier Robarts-Pépin discussion on PDF p. 2.

proposals.relationship: Morton questions whether Palmer’s Hamilton study substantiates its claims for working-class culture and historiographic novelty, while crediting its research on unions, conflict and politics.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1983 pp. 177–178 contrasts cultural interpretation with a traditional institutional account and questions transfer of Thompson’s model to heterogeneous Canada. Own 2000 pp. 23–25 revisits evidence and rhetoric, but p. 24 n. 50 says Palmer pp. 46–49 does not confirm Bercuson’s criticism. Bercuson, Ryerson, Armstrong and McNaught remain separate quoted critics, not Morton’s own original evidence. Complete Palmer books unread.
primary_locators: 1983 printed pp. 175–178, especially paragraph beginning L’un des reproches at the bottom of printed p. 176, continuing p. 177 and p. 178 first two paragraphs; 2000 printed pp. 23–25 and n. 50.

proposals.relationship: Morton questions the duration and breadth of working-class unity in Kealey’s Toronto interpretation and the claimed departure from institutional and political labour history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1983 pp. 175–178 praises Kealey’s book and recognizes his handling of sectarian complexity while questioning novelty and cultural transfer; own 2000 pp. 23–24 doubts that cross-sectarian unity lasted long. His 2000 pp. 25–27 credits the new historians’ durable empirical and regional gains. This is a distinct personal criticism already mediated in group edge 993, not removal or replacement of that qualified contribution.
primary_locators: 1983 printed pp. 175–178; 2000 printed pp. 23–24, sentence crossing the page break from If, as Kealey insisted through North America; pp. 25–27 qualifications.

proposals.relationship: Morton adopts Hobsbawm’s injunction to combine historical interpretation with efforts to change the world, applying it to his own reformist labour history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1983 and 2000 explicitly apply this purpose to nonrevolutionary historians including himself. Both cite Hobsbawm’s 1974 essay through Kealey and Peter Warrian’s 1976 Essays introduction; that intermediary credit remains. The original Hobsbawm essay is unread. Morton explicitly rejects revolutionary transformation in 2000 p. 13.
primary_locators: 1983 printed p. 166 paragraph beginning De telles préoccupations and n. 4; 2000 printed pp. 12–13 and n. 4.

proposals.relationship: Palmer supplies Morton with a practical prompt and a comparative-publication correction for his 2000 assessment of labour history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2000 p. 12 identifies Palmer’s May 2000 review of Russell Jacoby’s The End of Utopia as the immediate intellectual prompt. Morton says this may not be what either author intended and distinguishes his reformism on p. 13. Palmer’s review and Jacoby’s book are unread; invitation to publish alone is not the basis. On p. 26/n. 57 Morton also credits Palmer’s 12 June 2000 letter for the comparison that Labour/Le Travail’s French-publication record was better than the Canadian Historical Review’s. The letter itself is unread; this is Morton’s printed report, not independent verification of its counts.
primary_locators: 2000 printed p. 12, final main-text paragraph and n. 3; p. 13 opening paragraph.
2000 printed p. 26/n. 57, letter Bryan Palmer to author, 12 June 2000.

proposals.relationship: Palmer describes Morton’s Working People as uneven in quality, a criticism Morton himself reports and partly concedes.
proposals.evidence_note: Primary witness is Morton’s own 2000 p. 11/n. 2 quoting Palmer’s Working-Class Experience, second edition (1992), p. 418. Palmer’s original passage and the specific Working People edition it assesses remain unread/unconfirmed; no broader dismissal is inferred. Terry Copp retains credit for the 1980 work, while later Morton editions and Copp’s withdrawal are distinct.
primary_locators: 2000 printed p. 11 opening paragraph and n. 2, identifying Palmer 1992 p. 418.

proposals.relationship: Morton disputes Granatstein’s claim that Canadian history had been killed, pointing to successful teaching and strong public interest.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2002 article explicitly names his friend and coauthor, then rejects the death diagnosis while acknowledging problems in teaching. Friendship and collaborative work do not establish agreement; Granatstein’s 1998 book remains unread.
primary_locators: Policy Options 1 November 2002: paragraphs beginning Canadian ignorance of our history and To be fair, though Jack Granatstein, followed by People also kept telling us and the television examples.

proposals.relationship: Morton and Granatstein’s joint war histories connect combat experience with industrialization, rationing and the wider effects of the world wars on Canadian society.
proposals.evidence_note: Editorial comparison grounded in Tim Cook’s substantive 2003 review of their joint Canada and the Two World Wars. Cook identifies the two earlier books combined, praises integration and notes the bodies were not updated although the introduction is new. Joint authorship and reception do not establish intellectual influence or a division of labor. Full joint books unread.
primary_locators: Tim Cook, CBRA 2003 entry, complete three-paragraph review; especially paragraph beginning The measured, clear prose.

proposals.relationship: Morton notes that Parr’s Labouring Children necessarily reconstructs childhood largely through adult evidence, limiting recovery of children’s own voices.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2000 p. 33/n. 92 pairs Joy Parr’s Labouring Children (1980) with Neil Sutherland’s Children in English-Canadian Society (1976). Both retain credit; Morton calls the evidence limitation inevitable and places it within an otherwise positive assessment of feminist and family-history expansion. This is a qualified methodological limit, not rejection of Parr’s achievement or a claim to have read her full book.
primary_locators: Morton 2000 printed p. 33, final main-text questions on men-children/adolescents and n. 92 identifying Parr and Sutherland.
